title: Targeting CNS reservoirs with CAR/CXCR5 T cells for the long-term remission of HIV
text:
An HIV cure has proven elusive given the persistence of HIV in tissue sanctuaries in people with HIV on
suppressive anti-HIV drugs. A better understanding of the source of HIV rebound when anti-HIV drugs are halted
is needed in order to guide effective HIV cure strategies. Our long-term goals are 1) understanding HIV and SIV
reservoirs in both CD4 T cells and myeloid cells across the central nervous system (CNS) and lymphoid tissues,
2) developing a cellular immunotherapy using virus-specific chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells that target
tissue reservoirs of HIV in the CNS and lymphoid tissues that durably suppress HIV replication.

title: Advancing Proton Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy with Instantaneous Volumetric Imaging for Refractory Ventricular Tachycardia
text:
Ventricular tachycardia (VT) is a life-threatening heart rhythm disorder, and many patients are refractory to
medications or invasive procedures. Proton stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) offers a promising
noninvasive alternative, but its precision is challenged by complex heart motion, affecting radiation delivery
accuracy and safety. To address this, we propose developing real-time volumetric imaging for motion tracking
and dose delivery verification, ensuring safer and more effective proton SBRT for refractory VT patients.

title: Michigan Predoctoral Training in Genetics
text: The ever-changing landscape of genetic research requires the training of scientists in state-of-the-art genetics and genomics technologies to answer fundamental mechanistic biological questions that inform us about human biology and disease. The University of Michigan (UM) Predoctoral Genetics Training Program will consist of: (1) a cohort of Ph.D. trainees from six basic science departments spanning the UM Medical School and College of Literature, Sciences, and the Arts campuses; (2) productive faculty with research interests spanning a broad range of cutting-edge topics in genetics; and (3) a comprehensive curriculum in modern genetics. Here, we present our plan to train the next generation of genetics professionals through: (a) small group learning experiences; (b) faculty led and peer-to-peer discussions; (c) training grant specific activities that stress both the ethical conduct of science and critical importance of conducting rigorous and reproducible science; and (d) data driven evaluation, outcomes, mentoring, and career development programs.

title: Generation of new neurons in the aging adult brain: identifying mechanisms of adult neurogenesis by exploiting single cell spatial transcriptomics.
text:
Unlike many cell types in other tissues, neurons are not renewed during aging, with a very limited generation of
new neurons in young adults and none (or almost none) known to be produced in the aging mammalian nervous
system. Recently, I successfully converted dormant, radial glial-like and subependymal-like cells into new
functional neurons in the aged mouse neurogenic niches (subgranular and subventricular zone) by using a
therapeutically viable injection of an antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) to produce transient suppression of
synthesis of Polypyrimidine Tract Binding Protein (PTBP1). The research program I propose here will build
on that glia-to-neuron conversion coupled with combination of traditional single nuclear sequencing,
immunofluorescence and state-of-the-art single cell spatial transcriptomics (Multiplexed Error-Robust
Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization or MERFISH) to define and optimize the pathway(s) of generation of new
neurons in healthy and diseased brains produced by identity conversion from glial cells.

title: A Novel, AI-Enabled Dementia Care Agent to Reduce Disparities for Rural ADRD Care Partners.
text:
Care partners of individuals with Alzheimer’s Disease and Related Dementia (ADRD) in rural areas experience
higher caregiving burden and lower social support compared to urban caregivers. Although caregiver
education and support delivered by home and community-based service (HCBS) providers has demonstrated
the ability to reduce caregiver burden, those serving rural areas often face workforce shortages and capacity
constraints, limiting their service availability and accessibility among rural care partners. Further, no scalable
intervention currently exists to enable HCBS providers to deliver real-time education and support tailored to the
evolving needs of rural ADRD care partners.
In this proposed Fast Track, we will develop the AI-enabled Dementia Care Agent that will be available as a
24x7 service to support rural ADRD care partners and enhance the service capacity and accessibility among
rural HCBS providers. The Dementia Care Agent machine learning system will leverage a specialized knowledge
base, built from vetted, authoritative ADRD caregiving education and support content. Integrated with
CareVirtue’s proven caregiver support platform, it will deliver personalized ADRD education and support while
empowering rural HCBS providers to expand their capacity to support care partners effectively.

title: Stem cell and regeneration regulatory mechanisms in planarians
text:
Stem cells are important for public health because they are essential for the growth, maintenance, and repair
of tissues and lie at the heart of many cancers. Additionally, many regenerative medicine strategies propose
the utilization of stem cells to replace missing or undesirable cells. Planarians present a new and powerful
system to identify molecular mechanisms that regulate stem cells for regeneration.

title: Redefining C.difficile patient outcomes through network medicine
text:
The Centers for Disease Control and Infection consider Clostridioides difficile infection an urgent public health
threat; this career development award addresses our limited ability to predict its severe complications, response
to treatment, or recurrence of disease, and to distinguish it from indolent carriage. We hypothesize that by
integrating fecal immune, metabolic and microbial data, with modern bioinformatics tools, we can improve our
ability to predict these situations and understand the biological mechanisms behind them. Biological markers in
stool will be valuable tools to choose or design more timely and effective treatments for patients.

title: Tumor-Niche Co-evolution: Mechanisms Driving Ovarian Cancer Metastasis and Therapeutic Resistance
text:
Project Narratives
Successful anti-metastasis treatment is deeply rooted in our mechanistic understanding of the interactions between
disseminated tumor cells and the metastatic microenvironment. This study will use clonal barcoding and single cell
genomics to map cellular trajectories, identify key genes driving metastasis and chemoresistance, and uncover
interactions between tumor cells and the immune niche and extracellular matrix components. Ultimately, the findings
will inform the development of targeted therapies designed to overcome chemoresistance and improve outcomes for
patients with metastatic ovarian cancer.

title: Bioactive Lipid Mediators Core (BLMC)
text: The Bioactive Lipid Mediators Core (BLMC) is designed to support the ongoing work of affiliated scientists aiming to understand the systemic and neurophysiological outcomes of chronic drug use on lipid signaling. The focus on lipid biomarkers targets an emerging field that has unique promise to add a novel framework for understanding how lipid signaling in a wide range of tissues (e.g., plasma, CNS, liver, breast milk) is related to homeostatic dysregulation associated with the development and maintenance of drug use disorders. The Bradshaw lab has developed lipid extraction and analytical techniques aimed specifically at small molecule lipid metabolites like the endocannabinoids, lipoamines, prostaglandins, leukotrienes, and resolvins. These classes of lipids of have been shown to change in response to exposure to drugs of abuse and understanding this regulation has the potential to provide unique insight into how both acute and chronic drug use drives both systemic and central nervous system changes. This understanding would then drive the discovery of novel therapies to treat drug addiction. We will accomplish this by 1) Evaluation of plasma lipidomics patterns in multiple drug abuse models. Using animal models of drug use (THC, opioids, alcohol) we will use our optimized analytical techniques for analysis of bioactive lipid metabolite signaling molecules in plasma to determine how acute and chronic drug exposure causes systemic changes in these lipid classes. This analysis technique will then be used to determine how endogenous cannabinoid and related lipid signaling molecules changes in different disease states (PTSD, concussion, drug addiction) in human plasma. 2) Analyze sex difference in bioactive lipids in in targeted areas of the CNS with chronic drug use as a function of genetic sex. This will provide a novel framework to evaluate unique characteristics across and between drug models and sex. 3) Identification of changes in bioactive lipids in breast milk with exposure to drugs of abuse (THC, opioids). Lipidomics analysis of breastmilk in rodent models of drug use (THC, opioids) will provide a clearer understanding on how the presence of these drugs changes the lipid profile of breastmilk in a way that may have long term health consequences for offspring. 4) Develop data science analytical techniques of bioactive lipid metabolites to drive novel hypotheses on how drugs of abuse cause changes in systemic and CNS lipid signaling. Coupling the power of increasingly powerful analytical techniques with novel data mining and cluster analyses developed in-house will provide the field with new tools for interpreting lipid metabolomic information. 5) Increase the pipeline for IU undergraduate students to advance directly into STEM careers with a focus on mastering lipidomic, mass spectrometric, and bioinformatic techniques. Through this program, IU undergraduate students will be provided unique opportunities for training and research that are tailored to the field of lipidomics and mass spectrometry as well as multiple programmatic opportunities for professional development.

title: DRhQ Regulation of Intrinsic CD74 Activation in EAE
text:
Progressive multiple sclerosis (MS) is a devastating demyelinating autoimmune disease of the central nervous
system (CNS) that lacks effective therapies. Our laboratory has designed and is developing a new VA/OHSU
patented therapeutic, called DRhQ, that preserves myelinated axon integrity and function by interfering with a
key CD74-mediated inflammatory pathway involved in MS progression. We hypothesize that DRhQ binding to
cell-expressed CD74 not only competitively inhibits MIF binding to CD74, but also triggers its own signals that
prevent MIF-driven cleavage of the intracellular CD74 domain that leads to intranuclear production of
inflammatory factors that damage myelinated axons and promotes MS progression. Our proposed studies will
provide critical insight into this process.

title: Bioactive Injectable Implants for Functional Intervertebral Disc Regeneration
text:
Intervertebral disc degeneration is strongly implicated as a cause of low back pain. Current therapies
address the symptoms but do not restore native disc structure or function. Cell-mediated fibrotic changes to the
central nucleus pulposus are a defining characteristic of disc degeneration. The overall objective of this project
is arrest and reverse fibrotic changes in nucleus pulposus cells using a novel, extended-release RNA-based
therapy, and restore healthy disc structure and mechanical function in a preclinical large animal model.

title: Effect of Cannabis Use on Alcohol Craving and Consumption among those in Alcohol Treatment
text:
Cannabis is the most commonly used psychoactive substance among those with Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD),
yet there is a lack of data examining the direct impact of cannabis use on alcohol-related treatment outcomes.
This project will use ecological momentary assessment and transdermal alcohol biosensors to study the
momentary impact of cannabis use on alcohol craving and consumption in the natural environment among
those early in AUD treatment. Results from this research will have direct impact on cannabis messaging,
clinical decision-making, and intervention development for those with AUD.

title: Development of personalized healthy food incentives to improve diet and cardiovascular risk
text:
Title: Development of personalized healthy food incentives to improve diet and cardiovascular risk
PROJECT NARRATIVE
Diet has emerged as the leading risk factor for cardiovascular diseases responsible for substantial morbidity
and mortality among US adults. Despite the enormous human toll and fiscal burden of diet-related chronic
disease, population interventions have insufficiently addressed the complex determinants of this behavioral risk
factor. The proposed research strives to improve public health by applying advancements in machine learning
and qualitative research to better understand drivers of dietary decisions and using that insight to refine and
test an automated personalized healthy food incentive platform to improve healthy food purchases, diet quality,
and cardiovascular risk factors.

title: NOVEL DROSOPHILA TRANSCRIPTION FACTOR ORTHOLOG OF BCL11A/BCL11B IS CRUCIAL FOR REGULATING INTESTINAL STEM CELL QUIESCENCE AND PREVENTING GUT DYSFUNCTION DURING AGING
text:
Aging causes systematic changes in all cell types and tissues, predisposing organisms to a wide range of
diseases. Stem cell function is disrupted upon aging, unable to properly regulate the transition between
quiescence and active states, which can result in cancer or tissue degeneration. Using single-cell RNA
sequencing data, I have identified a novel regulator of intestinal stem cells called Chronophage, which is
required for maintenance of intestinal stem cells and contributes to gut pathologies when dysregulated.

title: Role for Semaphorin 3A in Microglial Activation and Alzheimer's Disease
text:
Alzheimer's disease, the primary cause of dementia in older adults, is characterized by various brain
changes including inflammation and neuronal loss. Microglia, specialized cells in the brain, are closely
involved in these processes and are influenced by certain genes associated with Alzheimer's risk. Our
recent findings suggest that SEMA3A, a protein involved in neuronal signaling, plays a role in activating
microglia and promoting the uptake of harmful substances like β-amyloid. Understanding this relationship
could lead to new strategies for treating Alzheimer's by targeting microglial activity.

title: Population Biology of African Malaria Vectors and Parasites
text: Malaria is a major public health problem, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, and advances in molecular biology, bioinformatics, and modeling offer new opportunities for vector control. Training the next generation of scientists to effectively use these technologies will strengthen malaria research capacity and accelerate control efforts in endemic regions. These efforts will also generate knowledge and tools that enhance surveillance, preparedness, and response to emerging mosquito-borne threats, helping to protect the health of Americans.

title: Genetically-encoded molecular imaging of genome-edited immune cells
text:
Bacterial metallophores are remarkable molecules that can chelate metals and also bind
to dedicated receptor proteins on the bacterial surface. We will design and develop a
chemogenetic platform in which the bacterial transporters would be ectopically expressed on
CAR-T cells to create a genetically-encoded reporter system to track genome-edited cells in vivo
at any depth, using nuclear imaging.

title: Integrative modelling of single-cell data to elucidate the genetic architecture of complex disease
text:
Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS) have identified thousands of common, non-coding variants
associated with disease. While integration of GWAS data with gene expression from bulk tissues has uncovered
some of the underlying genes and mechanisms, only a fraction of trait heritability can be explained by existing
bulk datasets and the majority of GWAS loci do not colocalize with QTLs from bulk expression data.
Understanding which cell types and contexts are the most relevant for a given disease – both at the level of
individual loci and across the genome – is thus critical to moving from individual variants to an understanding of
broader processes and, eventually, to effective interventions.

title: High-throughput Liquid Chromatograph Triple Quadrupole Mass Spectrometer
text: Automation and increased sensitivity of triple quadrupole mass spectrometers have revolutionized biomedical and environmental health research with the ability to quantify target biomolecules, metabolites, biomarkers, and contaminants over a vast dynamic range, mid part per-quadrillion- to high part-per-billion. This application seeks to acquire a high throughput liquid chromatograph triple quadrupole at Wayne State University to significantly augment research productivity on the Wayne State University campus and in the regional community.

title: Models and Algorithms for Biological Networks and Polymers: Stochastic Probability Landscape and Chromatin Ensembles
text:
Program Director/Principal Investigator (Liang, Jie):
Project Narrative
We will develop computational models and tools to construct probability landscapes of networks of
stochastically interacting proteins, DNA/RNAs, and other molecules, and to quantify the flow maps of
fluxes and the exact topology of these landscapes, so their behavior and roles in influencing cellular
phenotypes can be better understood. In addition, we will study the biophysics of 3D genome folding,
and will develop computational tools based on polymer modeling to identify the minimal sets of
genomic driver interactomes that dictate the 3D conformations of chromatin loci and identify those
that persists across tissues and those that are formed adaptively in different cell types.
